about: Every pot of money the town and the schools hold outside the voted budget, as a balance at each 30 June, and whether it is growing.

conclusions.basis: `special-revenue-read.csv` (FY2011-FY2023, ties to every printed total); `munis-school-ytd.csv` period 13 (FY2024-FY2026); proved against `school-special-revenue-fy26-q3.csv`.
conclusions.claim: The schools’ fee, choice, lunch and circuit-breaker funds held $1,167,744 at 30 June 2026.
conclusions.detail: The same fourteen funds every year, from $483,815 at 30 June 2011. Through FY2023 each balance is the annual report’s own; after it, the 30 June 2023 balance is carried through the period-13 ledgers, and the 30 June 2025 result matches the Town’s March 2026 report to the cent for every fund. The grant funds are not in this total.

last.unit: held by the same fourteen school funds, 30 June 2026

conclusions.not_shown: What the balances were spent on, or whether a lower balance means a programme cost more, took in less, or was deliberately drawn down.
conclusions.so_what: They rose to $2,170,682 in FY2022 and have fallen since: not growing now.

conclusions.basis: `free-cash-history-fincom.csv` (the Town’s fact sheet) checked against `free-cash-proof.csv` (the Division of Local Services).
conclusions.claim: Certified free cash rose from $263,188 at the FY2015 close to $3,354,370 at the FY2025 close.
conclusions.detail: Not a steady climb: it fell in 3 of 10 years and rose in 7. The state’s own proof agrees with every figure it covers. Free cash is not held by any department: Town Meeting appropriates it. The Town’s FY27 budget release cites a state guide of 5-7% of its annual budget.

last.unit: certified free cash, as of 1 July 2025

conclusions.not_shown: Whether the balance is too high or too low: the guide is a range, and how much of each year’s free cash was then appropriated is in /analysis/free-cash, not here.
conclusions.so_what: 6.65% of the prior year’s budget by the Town’s own count, against 0.81% then. Spent only by Town Meeting.

conclusions.basis: `munis-school-ytd.csv`, report gf-school, period 13, `available_budget` summed; the free cash proof’s line CL#11.
conclusions.claim: The school general fund closed FY2026 with $482,118 unspent; FY2025 with $627,117.
conclusions.detail: $106,827 in FY2023 and $215,776 in FY2024, so the last two years are larger. A further $236,767 was still committed to open purchase orders at the FY2026 close. The state’s free cash proof adds unspent, uncommitted appropriations back as one of its lines, which is how this money reaches free cash.

y26.unit: unspent in the school general fund at the FY2026 close

conclusions.not_shown: Why more was left in FY2025 and FY2026; which accounts it sat in is in the FY25 and FY26 school surplus reports.
conclusions.so_what: Not kept by the schools: the state’s free cash calculation adds unspent appropriations back for the town.

conclusions.claim: The schools were $627,117 of the $2,457,761 the town left unspent at the FY2025 close.
conclusions.detail: 17.6% at the FY2024 close and 18.1% at the FY2023 close. Two documents, set side by side: the state’s proof prints one town-wide line, and the school figure is department 300’s own ledger. The remainder is everything else the town appropriated, which nothing published splits by department.

share.unit: of the town’s unspent appropriations at the FY2025 close was the schools’

conclusions.not_shown: Which town departments or articles make up the remainder: registered as a gap, closed by a departmental turnback schedule.
conclusions.so_what: 25.5% — the rest of the general fund left the larger part, and no published document says which departments.

conclusions.basis: `free-cash-proof.csv`, line CL#6, Lunenburg; Finance Committee minutes of 28 May 2026.
conclusions.claim: Receipts above the town’s estimate added over $1,000,000 a year to free cash, FY2022–FY2025.
conclusions.detail: The state’s proof shows between $1,006,025 and $1,363,025 a year. On 28 May 2026 a Finance Committee member said the town had not collected less than four million in local receipts in ten years, against an estimate of 3.535 million. Why the estimate is set where it is is a hypothesis here; nothing tests it.

min.unit: the smallest of those years’ receipts above estimate

conclusions.not_shown: Whether the margin is deliberate caution, receipts that grew faster than anyone could forecast, or one-time money; each fits the same line.
conclusions.so_what: Where the town sets its revenue estimate is a decision, and it decides part of how big free cash gets.

conclusions.basis: `special-revenue-read.csv`, FY2011-FY2023, non-school funds, split by name.
conclusions.claim: Of $8,277,392 in town special revenue funds at 30 June 2023, 86% was ARPA or utility money.
conclusions.detail: Federal relief $3,337,921 and enterprises $3,800,195. Everything else the town held in special revenue came to $1,139,277, against $813,012 at 30 June 2011. Later years are printed in a different table this project has not yet read.

pct.unit: of town special revenue at 30 June 2023 was federal relief or enterprise

conclusions.not_shown: What the town funds held at 30 June 2024, 2025 or 2026: registered as a gap.
conclusions.so_what: Federal relief with federal deadlines, and water, sewer, trash and cable money kept for ratepayers.

conclusions.claim: The general stabilization fund grew from $1,186,777 in FY2011 to $2,901,158 in FY2024.
conclusions.detail: Year-end cash, each year closed on the identities its own table prints. The special-purpose stabilization funds are counted separately in /analysis/stabilization-funds.

last.unit: in the general stabilization fund, 30 June 2024

conclusions.not_shown: How much of the growth is deposits voted by Town Meeting and how much is interest.
conclusions.so_what: A reserve by design: spending it takes a two-thirds vote of Town Meeting.

conclusions.basis: `special-revenue-read.csv` (“50/50 Grant Sped Tuitions”), then fund 2640 in `munis-school-ytd.csv`; identified by FY2023 receipts equal to the cent.
conclusions.claim: The circuit breaker fund closed FY2026 at $281,806, down from $482,004 at its FY2020 high.
conclusions.detail: The state reimburses part of high-cost special education after the year; the district may carry it forward. In March 2024 the district told the Finance Committee a tuition rise was probably absorbed by circuit breaker carry-over, which is why the account had gone down.

last.unit: in the circuit breaker fund, 30 June 2026

conclusions.not_shown: Which children’s costs the carry-over paid for in any year.
conclusions.so_what: It fell in 5 of the 6 years since: received and spent, not piling up.
